P1.evidence: Same open the rep uses everywhere: 'Luke, I seen your application. It's very interesting. And I'm kind of an old school guy. So walk me through, like, what's the main thing you're trying to fix and how can we actually help you with?' The application is named but never read back, so the prospect gets no sense of having been read. No four-part frame and no frame agreement anywhere in the call, which matters here — with no agreed structure, the prospect set the agenda himself at 00:21:54 by asking for the cost, and the rep had to bat it away.

P2.evidence: The strongest baseline in the batch on the lifestyle side. Work was worked properly — 'You're an attorney, right? So you probably have less time than more time' followed by a real dig into the three-hour commute. Results from current training came out of 'would you say that you're in good shape right now?' ('cardiovascular-wise, I'm not in good shape'). Diet was taken day by day, sleep was asked directly ('what's your schedule of sleep and how do you actually feel when you're waking up?') and energy followed it. What is missing is the hard data: age was volunteered ('I'll be 45 years old this year'), weight fell out of the nutrition answer ('right now I'm like 215'), height was never captured at all, and health conditions and hereditary history were never asked as a question — only injuries were. Training frequency was probed sideways ('So you're working out in the morning?') without ever establishing actual days trained.

P3.evidence: The family drive-through worked: 'So you have three kids... You're not tossing around on the floor with them?', 'Are you active with them, too?', then 'you don't want to be that dad that sits on the couch and, like, he needs to be taken care of, right?' and 'That's the thing I'm talking about. You know, like you're leading by example.' Both reflect-backs landed — 'we're playing the longevity game here, not chasing some athletic goal here' drew 'this is a marathon, not a sprint for me', and 'we're getting you from good to great' was accepted. But the two deepest moves were replaced by assertion rather than question: instead of asking what moving better would do for him, the rep told him what other clients report — 'they text me after two months and they're like, man, I'm more confident. My relationships got better.' Nothing was asked about a physical thing he wants to do and can't, which was available and free — he avoids jiu-jitsu because of his back.

P4.evidence: Asked the opening question cleanly — 'What have you tried so far?' — and got an unusually rich answer: CrossFit, a CrossFit-lite sweat class, the Mayhem Athlete app he pays for himself, THENX, pure powerlifting, bodybuilding, yoga. Then stopped. The prospect had already handed over the diagnosis — 'I just feel like I've been jumping in and out of so many different programs' — and the rep never asked why it didn't stick, never asked what is actually in the way, and never had him name the gap in his own words. This is the phase that would have built the value case against the cheap substitutes, and skipping it is why there was nothing to argue with when the price landed.

P5.evidence: Only a fragment ran, and it ran as a statement rather than a question: 'you don't want to be that dad that sits on the couch and, like, he needs to be taken care of, right?' The prospect agreed and it went nowhere. Never asked what two years of nothing changing looks like, never asked whether he is willing to settle for it, never asked why not, never asked for a line in the sand. For a 44-year-old with a 14-year herniated disc, an unrepaired shoulder tear and collapsing recovery, the cost of inaction was sitting right there and was not touched.

P6.evidence: Both commitment questions were asked close to script. 'If you had this right training, simple nutrition, and accountability from Trevor, everything built around your life, do you feel like you would get to your goals?' — 'Yeah, I do.' Then 'if you can figure out all the logistical details, are you fully committed to showing up and doing the work?' — 'Yep.' He got a clear yes before presenting price. Two caveats a coach should note: the second question was prefaced with 'I don't think I need to ask you that', which pre-answers it and cheapens the yes; and both commitment checks came AFTER the three pillars had been presented, inverting the script's whole point of securing commitment before presenting anything. The yes was also worth very little because P4 and P5 never ran, so there was no accumulated cost behind it — it evaporated the instant a number was attached.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted and refused, so payment and onboarding were never reachable. Noted for completeness: the rep did make a secondary sale attempt on the $200/month Primal University tier and ran none of the equivalent steps on it either — the Skool link was pasted in the chat, no payment was taken, nothing was scheduled, and the prospect left saying he would look at it later in the day.

objection_plays.detail: The clearest money trigger in the batch and the play was not run at all. Prospect: 'I was thinking this was going to be much less expensive than this' and then 'I'm not going to pay $6,000 a month for this.' Of the scripted moves, zero ran. No isolation — 'finances aside, is there anything else keeping you from being 100% in' was never asked, so the rep never established whether price was the real blocker. No 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place'. No mention that most clients pay upfront but some break it up, and no payment plan floated at any point. No permission question about discussing finances honestly, and therefore none of the six financial-picture questions — cash on hand, monthly surplus, credit cards, available credit, used versus available, investments. The rep asked one question, 'do you feel like getting to your goals is worth $6,000, or it's not worth $6,000 for you?', accepted the deflection, and then within about ninety seconds produced a $200/month product and told the prospect his own number was 'almost on point'. Elapsed time from full price to downsell is under four minutes.

The 'a cheaper alternative already worked for me' gap, already logged in the playbook against the Badrane Hriouch call, recurs here in its purest form. This prospect pays for a CrossFit membership, a Mayhem Athlete subscription and a physical therapist, and has run THENX, powerlifting, bodybuilding and yoga off his own back. He was explicit: 'I think there's other paths for me to pursue rather than just pay $6,000 for this.' There is no scripted play for it, and the rep did not improvise one — he had the counter-argument in his own notes (every one of those substitutes had already failed to stick, which is why the prospect filled in the form) and never used it. Note also that the rep's own downsell became the cheaper alternative, which converts a script gap into a self-inflicted one.

notes: Discovery-heavy, close-light: baseline and family motivation were handled well, then the two phases that build willingness to pay — root cause and consequence — were skipped entirely, and the price landed on an unbuilt foundation. The single coachable moment is the four minutes after 00:36:13: no isolation, no payment plan, no financial picture, and a $200/month product volunteered in response to the prospect's own anchor. Second priority: when a prospect misstates the price as monthly, correct it before doing anything else.
